I look at stones, not people.

Of the twelve stones, eleven are glass; good glass, 1980s work. Only one is a real emerald, the smallest. I told the treasurer on Monday. ‘So the stones stolen in 1987 never came back,’ he said. He wrote it on a piece of paper and put it in his pocket.

Amparo Soto — interview

A file reopened from the archive (March 1987, closed as ‘perpetrator unknown, items recovered’):

· The twelve emeralds in the crown of the statue of the Virgin were stolen from the chapel. That year’s treasurer of the brotherhood: Ignacio Lara.
· A month later Ignacio Lara reported that he had bought the stones back from ‘an anonymous intermediary’; the price, 38 million pesetas, was paid with a donation from the Fundación Santa Ana.
· The stones were put back without being valued; the record says ‘at the request of the brotherhood’s president’.
· Adviser’s signature on the foundation’s 1987 donation decision: ‘Dr E. Varga’.
The 1987 file closed as a ‘miracle’ has been reopened.
THE 1987 FILE — THE CROWN’S EMERALDS

· Cause of death: two blows to the top of the head, from above, with a heavy, angular object. Silver polishing paste in the wounds.
· No fractures consistent with a fall; hips, wrists and shoulders intact.
· Time of death: 21.00–22.30.
AUTOPSY REPORT

· The scaffold’s brakes are locked, its guardrail in place; no footprints on the upper platform, the dust undisturbed.
· Of the six silver candlesticks on the altar, one is freshly polished, the others dusty. Luminol: blood in the grooves of its base.
· In the victim’s pocket, a piece of paper: ‘11 of 12 stones are glass. 1987.’

Ignacio Lara’s house (with the branch chief’s approval):

· In the study, silver polishing paste and a bloodstained cloth; the blood is the victim’s.
· In the safe, a letter dated 1987, in Spanish, unsigned, typewritten: ‘The stones are in Zurich. In return, the presidency. The glass arrives on Friday.’
· From the Fundación Santa Ana, an ‘honorary advisory’ payment to Ignacio Lara every Holy Week since 1987.
IGNACIO LARA’S HOUSE — SEARCH
President of the brotherhood.
The brotherhood’s affairs stay within the brotherhood.
No.
In 1987 I saved the stones. The brotherhood was grateful to me.

I took the stones, in 1987; I had debts. A lady came from the foundation and said, ‘We’ll buy them back, you’ll become president.’ We put in the glass. Fernando said, ‘Before Holy Week I’ll tell the brothers.’ I took the candlestick. Afterwards I polished it and put it back. The Virgin saw; I didn’t want anyone else to see.
You struck Fernando with the candlestick.
Briefly. I asked Fernando about the Holy Week budget; he was on the scaffold. I left at half past nine. He was old, the scaffold is narrow; he fell.
He straightens the medal on his chest.

I polish the candlesticks, every week. I polished one; what of it?

On the morning of 18 October 2030, in a brotherhood chapel in Triana, the brotherhood’s treasurer Fernando Ibáñez (59) was found dead at the foot of the procession float. Beside him, a wheeled cleaning scaffold.

The capataz Paco Romero found the body at 07.30 when he opened the chapel. The brotherhood’s president Ignacio Lara said, ‘He fell from the scaffold.’ That week the crown’s emeralds were being valued by the jeweller Amparo Soto.

The jeweller told of the glass, the capataz of who stayed inside that evening and of the 1987 ‘miracle’; those got the archive opened. The chapel examination found the untouched scaffold and the one shiny candlestick. The house search gave the cloth and the 1987 letter.
The best place to hide a candlestick is the altar.
Triana — October 2030

In 1987 the brotherhood’s treasurer Ignacio Lara sold the crown’s emeralds to pay his debts; a month later the stones ‘recovered’ with Fundación Santa Ana money were glass, and Ignacio became president. When today’s treasurer Fernando Ibáñez learned of the glass at the valuation, he decided to tell the brothers. Ignacio struck him in the chapel with a silver candlestick, polished it and put it back on the altar.
Who killed Fernando Ibáñez?
